How to say no to a client politely (without losing the project): 4 decline scripts with a "yes, if..." option

2026-11-26

A lot of advice on saying no to a client stops at "be polite and be firm". True, but not much help when you're looking at an enquiry you don't want, a request you can't fit in, or a budget that doesn't cover the work.

What helps is knowing which kind of no you're giving. A project that's the wrong fit, a month with no room, a request outside the agreed work and a budget that's too small are four different conversations. Treat them the same and the client gets a vague brush-off.

Below are four short decline scripts, one per case. Each comes with a "yes, if..." alternative: a version of the work you'd genuinely be glad to do, so the client has somewhere to go other than away.

Not legal advice. These are emails, not contract terms. If you're declining something that a signed contract already commits you to, read the contract first: that's a different conversation from turning down new work.

First, decide which no it is

Before you write a word, sort the situation: what's actually stopping you from saying yes?

The reason What the client needs to hear The "yes, if..." you might offer
Wrong fit This isn't work you do (or do well), so they'll be better served elsewhere The part of it you do well, or a name to try
No capacity You'd like to, but not on their timeline A later start date, or a smaller first piece now
Out of scope It isn't part of the current project, and you won't add it inside the current one A separate piece of work later, or a swap
Budget The work they described doesn't fit the money they have A smaller scope that does fit, or the project in phases

If two reasons apply, lead with the one that's most useful to the client. "I'm booked until March" gives them something to act on.

What a polite no contains

Polite doesn't mean long. A good decline usually fits in five or six sentences, and it does four things:

  1. Thanks them for something specific. "Thanks for sending the brief" beats "thanks for reaching out": it shows you read it.
  2. Puts the decision near the top. If the no is buried in the third paragraph, the client has to hunt for it. Say it by the second sentence.
  3. Gives one honest reason, briefly. One reason is plenty. A list of reasons reads like you're arguing with yourself, and invites the client to argue with each one.
  4. Offers a "yes, if..." you'd keep. This is the part that keeps the relationship. It has to be real: an offer you'd accept if they took it tomorrow.

Skip the apology spiral ("I'm so sorry, I feel terrible"). One "sorry" is fine. Three turn a business decision into something the client has to comfort you about.

The free piece: four decline scripts

Copy, adapt and make them sound like you. Square brackets are yours to fill in. Every name and project here is invented.

1. Wrong fit

Use this when the work isn't what you do, or not what you want your business to do more of.

Hi [NAME],

Thanks for sending over the details of [PROJECT]. I've read them
through, and I'm going to pass on this one: [TYPE OF WORK] isn't
an area I work in, and you deserve someone who does it every week.

Yes, if it helps: I could take on [THE PART YOU DO], for example
[SPECIFIC PIECE], and work alongside whoever handles the rest.
If you'd rather keep it with one person, [NAME / TYPE OF SPECIALIST]
is who I'd look for.

Either way, good luck with it.

[YOUR NAME]

Why it works. "Isn't an area I work in" is a fact about you, not a judgment about their project. The partial offer only works if the job splits cleanly (say, a copywriter writing the site words while someone else builds it). If it doesn't, cut that paragraph and keep the referral. Only recommend people you'd vouch for.

2. No capacity

Use this when you'd take the project at another time.

Hi [NAME],

Thanks for thinking of me for [PROJECT]. It looks like a good one,
but I can't take it on for a [MONTH] start: my schedule is full
until [DATE], and I'd rather say so now than squeeze it in badly.

Yes, if your timing can move: I could start on [DATE], and I'm
happy to hold that slot until [DAY] while you check.
Or, if something has to happen sooner, I could do [SMALLER PIECE,
e.g. the outline / the homepage only] before then, and the rest
from [DATE].

Let me know which, if either, works for you.

[YOUR NAME]

Why it works. "I'd rather say so now" frames the no as looking after their project. Holding a slot until a named day gives them a reason to decide without fake urgency: the date is real and you set it. Don't offer the smaller piece if fitting it in would put your current clients' work at risk.

3. Out of scope

Use this mid-project, when a request is big enough that you won't fold it in and you don't want to add it to this project at all, even for a fee. (If you'd do it for a price, the out-of-scope request email guide covers how to sort and quote it.)

Hi [NAME],

Thanks for suggesting [REQUEST]. It makes sense that it's come up
at this stage.

I'm going to keep it out of the current project, though. It isn't
in the scope we agreed on [DATE], and adding it now would put
[THE AGREED DELIVERABLE / THE LAUNCH DATE] at risk.

Yes, if we treat it as its own piece of work: once [CURRENT
PROJECT] is signed off, I'll send a short proposal for it.
Or, if it matters more than something already planned, tell me
which item it should replace and I'll check whether the swap fits.

[YOUR NAME]

Why it works. The no protects something the client already wants: the thing you're building for them now. The swap option hands the trade-off back to them, which is where it belongs. If they pick a swap, write down what was removed.

4. Budget

Use this when the money and the brief don't match, and you'd still like the work.

Hi [NAME],

Thanks for being upfront about the budget for [PROJECT]. That
makes this easier.

I can't deliver everything in the brief for [THEIR BUDGET]. Doing
it properly would be closer to [YOUR PRICE], and I'd rather tell
you that than cut corners you'd only find later.

Yes, if we change the shape of it. For [THEIR BUDGET] I could do:
- [ITEM A]
- [ITEM B]
and leave [ITEM C] for a second phase, or for you to handle
in-house.

Would that version be useful, or is the full brief the priority?

[YOUR NAME]

Why it works. You don't lower your price; you reduce the work to fit their budget. That keeps your rate intact and gives the client something concrete to say yes to. If no smaller version would be worth doing, skip the "yes, if" and close with a polite pass.

Where a "yes, if..." goes wrong

The alternative is what makes these emails work. It's also where they can backfire:

  • An offer you don't mean. If you'd groan when they accept, don't make it.
  • A discount instead of a smaller job. "I could do it for a bit less" suggests your first number wasn't real. Change the work, not the rate.
  • A vague "maybe later". "Get in touch in the new year" puts all the effort on them. A date, a held slot or a named second phase is something they can act on.
  • Conditions you won't track. If you hold a slot until Friday, check on Friday.

The same applies to extra rounds of feedback: a "yes, if..." for one more round is easiest when your proposal already said how many were included. The revision limits guide has wording for that.

When they push back

Sometimes the reply is "Are you sure? It's only a small project" or "Could you do it for [LOWER NUMBER]?"

  • Answer once, with the same reason. "I'm sure. My schedule is full until [DATE], but that start date is still open" is enough.
  • Keep negotiation out of long threads. If they want to explore the "yes, if", suggest a short call, then confirm what you agreed in writing.
  • Let silence be an answer. You don't need to chase. They know where the door is.

Making the next no easier

Many declines feel hard because the client didn't see them coming. Three habits help:

  • Say how you work early. Your enquiry reply can mention your usual lead time and the projects you take on, so some clients who don't fit rule themselves out.
  • Ask about budget before you write a proposal. A range is fine, and a budget decline is gentler at the enquiry stage than after a long proposal.
  • Agree scope in writing. A confirmed scope summary turns an out-of-scope no into "here's the line we agreed" rather than your word against theirs.

The limits

  • No script keeps every client. Some will go elsewhere, however well you word it.
  • Tone varies. Read each script aloud and change anything that doesn't sound like you.
  • They're not contract advice. Turning down new work is your call. Refusing work you've already agreed to deliver is a contract question.
